# Conclusion

Whether land ownership is necessary or sufficient for superior farm performance is a question aggregate productivity comparisons cannot settle, because they fold together the technology a farmer is able to reach and the efficiency with which that technology is used. Separating the two across five rounds of the Ghana Living Standards Survey, for `r fmt_num(N_ALL, 0)` farm households compared under similar observable conditions, returns the same answer on both counts at the aggregate: landowners and matched non-owners differ by less than one percentage point on every measure. Non-owners sit marginally closer to the best available technology, owners are marginally more efficient against their own frontier, and on the measure combining the two the advantages very nearly cancel.

That near-parity is produced by offsetting rather than by sameness, and the distinction carries most of what follows. Across the disaggregations the group leading on reaching the frontier technology is repeatedly not the group leading on using it, though the pattern is not universal: all five education categories show it, as do half the regions and both extremes of the crop panel. Schooling is the cleanest case, widening the ownership advantage in technology access while widening the non-ownership advantage in efficiency, so that the two gradients cross rather than one dominating. Where the channels instead point the same way the combined gap is no longer small. Greater Accra, the one region in which non-owners lead on both, carries a meta-efficiency gap of more than six percentage points, several times anything the aggregate comparison reports. Near-parity is therefore a statement about how two channels combine, not a finding that ownership bears on neither.

The input record shows the same division from the quantity side. On land of comparable size and cropping, landowners harvest between `r fmt_num(fig1_range("Output (real value)", min), 1)` and `r fmt_num(fig1_range("Output (real value)", max), 1)` percent more per hectare than matched non-owners while using less of every input measured, and the shortfall widens systematically from what a household already commands to what a market transaction must supply: between `r fmt_num(abs(fig1_range("Household labor (AE)", max)), 1)` and `r fmt_num(abs(fig1_range("Household labor (AE)", min)), 1)` percent on household labour, but between `r fmt_num(abs(fig1_range(c("Fertilizer (Kg/ha)","Pesticide (Liter/ha)","Planting materials (real value)","Hired labor (man-days/ha)"), max)), 0)` and `r fmt_num(abs(fig1_range(c("Fertilizer (Kg/ha)","Pesticide (Liter/ha)","Planting materials (real value)","Hired labor (man-days/ha)"), min)), 0)` percent across fertilizer, pesticide, planting material, and hired labour. Non-owners farm more intensively on precisely the purchased inputs from which they draw the higher marginal return. Whatever ownership secures in this setting, a greater command of purchased inputs is not it.

Disaggregating ownership sharpens the aggregate result rather than qualifying it. Documented owners and holders of transferable or collateral rights fall `r fmt_num(100*min(abs(c(tbl_num("table4.csv","Owned with documentation","c3"), tbl_num("table4.csv","Can be used as collateral security","c3"), tbl_num("table4.csv","Can be sold","c3"), tbl_num("table4.csv","Can be used as collateral security and sold","c3")))), 0)` to `r fmt_num(100*max(abs(c(tbl_num("table4.csv","Owned with documentation","c3"), tbl_num("table4.csv","Can be used as collateral security","c3"), tbl_num("table4.csv","Can be sold","c3"), tbl_num("table4.csv","Can be used as collateral security and sold","c3")))), 0)` percentage points short of matched non-owners in meta-frontier efficiency, and the shortfall grows with how complete those rights are rather than shrinking. Mode of acquisition splits the two channels instead of reversing them: on rented, purchased, and family-allocated land owners sit closer to the frontier technology yet trail comparable non-owners by `r fmt_num(100*abs(max(unlist(lapply(objs$acq[c("rented","purchased","kinship")], function(x) x$te)))), 0)` to `r fmt_num(100*abs(min(unlist(lapply(objs$acq[c("rented","purchased","kinship")], function(x) x$te)))), 0)` percentage points in technical efficiency, a cost large enough to outweigh the access advantage. Only on land accessed free of charge do owners perform at least as well on every measure. No tenure form delivers a uniform advantage, and the direction of the ownership gap turns out to be a property of which dimension is examined rather than a stable feature of ownership itself.

Nor is the configuration a fixed feature of the period. Over the three rounds whose sampling frames support comparison, landowners hold a modest technology advantage throughout while the non-ownership efficiency advantage narrows from `r fmt_num(abs(trend_gap("TE", "GLSS5")), 1)` percentage points in 2005/06 to `r fmt_num(abs(trend_gap("TE", "GLSS7")), 1)` by 2016/17, almost all of it in the final interval. Combining the two, meta-frontier efficiency crosses from a small landowner deficit to a small landowner advantage without ever departing more than `r fmt_num(trend_range("MTE", c("GLSS5","GLSS6","GLSS7"), function(v) max(abs(v))), 1)` percentage points from zero. Convergence on the efficiency margin alongside a persistent but modest access advantage describes a decoupling of ownership from performance rather than a reversal of it.

Several features of the design bound these conclusions, and Section 5 states where each one binds. Matching balances the two groups on what the survey records and cannot reach selection on what it does not, so land quality, managerial ability, and standing within the institutions that allocate land remain capable of entering the estimates as though they were consequences of ownership; every gap reported here is an association rather than an effect. Tenure is self-reported and, where customary and statutory conceptions of ownership diverge, contested rather than merely mismeasured. The tenure detail is unevenly available across rounds, so the disaggregated contrasts rest on narrower foundations than the aggregate. Most consequentially, the aggregate gap is small enough that its sign is not identified: it reverses under the assumed distribution of the inefficiency term, under some matching algorithms and aggregation rules, when the average is restricted to the three rounds sharing a comparable frame, and it turns as well on the decision to weight each survey round equally regardless of its size. The near-parity is robust throughout; its direction is not, and nothing concluded here rests on it.

Within those bounds the findings bear on three live policy questions. The first is the reach of land redistribution and titling: neither margin carries a measurable performance premium in these data, which places the productivity returns to those instruments alone below what is commonly assumed and directs attention to the conditions that would have to accompany them. The second is the targeting of technology programmes, from input subsidies to mechanisation services and extension. Farmers operating without ownership are not less efficient users of the technology they can reach, so their thinner access to purchased inputs reflects the terms on which those inputs are available rather than any deficit in capability. The third is uniformity of design: the association between tenure and performance changes direction across regions and crops, which bears directly on whether a single national instrument is the right shape for the problem.

Future work should pursue the causal mechanisms this design cannot isolate, using panel or experimental variation capable of separating tenure from the conditions that travel with it, and should examine how finance, infrastructure, and market linkages interact with tenure in shaping productivity. The reversal documented here, in which documentation and transfer rights track lower rather than higher meta-frontier efficiency, is not explained by this design and merits direct investigation.

The question posed at the outset admits a two-part answer. Ownership is not necessary for reaching the technology available in Ghanaian agriculture, because rental, sharecropping, and borrowing already move land toward farmers able to work it, and non-owners reach the frontier as closely as owners do. Nor is it sufficient for using that technology well, because holding land, documenting it, and holding the right to sell or pledge it carry no efficiency premium over comparable non-owners, and on several margins carry a penalty. Secure tenure operates in this setting as one input among several rather than as the condition on which productivity turns. That does not make land policy unimportant. It locates its value somewhere other than in the productivity gains titling is expected to deliver, and directs attention to the input, credit, and market conditions that determine what any farmer, owner or not, can do with the land they work.
